name: Daria Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my grandparents' farm, Ashgrove, which is ninety hectares of barley and oats, twenty beef cattle that my grandfather won't part with, an old apple orchard and my goats. I started the goats four years ago with twelve kids, and now there are sixty milkers. I milk at six, do the cheese in the little dairy room by nine, and then help with whatever the farm needs, which this month is muck spreading and fixing the orchard fence the deer keep breaking. Evenings are packing orders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the goat side work, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandparents pay me a wage for the farm work, and the cheese is meant to be my own little business inside the farm, though most of the profit goes back into it. I sell online and to three delis, and I use AI every day, for the website, the order emails, working out salt and rennet amounts, even planning the posts with photos of the goats. I'm single and I live in the back rooms of the farmhouse, which keeps costs low, and I've got about four months saved. On Sundays I drive my grandmother to Mass, because she doesn't like driving in the dark anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, it's a good tool and that's all. I'd post something about how my AI writes a better order email than I do, but it still can't make cheese. People like that sort of thing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me fine. I'm already getting the useful bits out of it, so if it stays like this, I'm ahead of most small producers. The farm goes on, the goats go on, and I keep building the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more money into the dairy room, maybe a second vat for about four thousand, and grow to two more delis in the city. I'd keep using AI for the marketing and the paperwork. I'd also try to persuade my grandfather to let me turn some of the barley into a fodder crop for the goats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your grandfather feel about the AI tools you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I'm talking to myself. He'll stand behind me while I'm at the laptop and say, ask it what the barley price will be next year. And I tell him, it doesn't know, Grandpa, nobody knows. He seems pleased by that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good week look like for the cheese business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty orders online, the delis all reordering, and no goat with mastitis, which is an infection in the udder. Last Christmas I sold out of the ash-coated cheese in four days. That week I felt like a real business owner, not just the granddaughter.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool and that's all, and post that my AI writes a better order email than I do but still can't make cheese.
S0.think: It'd suit me fine, because I already get the useful parts out of it and I'm ahead of most small producers. The farm and the goats carry on and I keep building the cheese business.
S0.do: Puts about four thousand into a second cheese vat and grows to two more city delis. Keeps using AI for marketing and paperwork, and tries to persuade her grandfather to grow fodder for the goats.
S0.feel: Calm, and impatient to get on with it.
S0.quote: He'll stand behind me while I'm at the laptop and say, ask it what the barley price will be next year.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is an enterprising young producer who uses AI daily and sees a plateau as leaving her ahead of her peers. Her pride comes from building a business of her own inside the family farm. Her grandfather's scepticism is affectionate rather than hostile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small farms that move early. People who sit and complain will get left behind, and the ones who pick up the new tools will do fine. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. There are already small robotic milking units for goats, and if I could get one, I could run a hundred goats on my own and spend my time on the cheese and the customers. The worry is my grandparents, because the barley and cattle side doesn't make much money already, and it'd make even less if big farms go robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd look at a second-hand robotic milker, maybe twenty-five thousand with a farm loan, and test the AI tools that predict mastitis from the milk readings. I'd talk to Grandpa about renting the barley land to a bigger neighbour with the machines, so the farm earns from it without us having to buy expensive kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, actually, though I feel the weight of the farm a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on a loan of twenty-five thousand with four months of savings. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd lie awake over it once or twice. But the goats pay for themselves if I sell enough cheese, and I've got the numbers from three years of sales. My grandmother says nothing good was ever built without a loan, and she should know, she paid off this farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your grandfather take renting out the barley land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. He'd say his father never let anyone else farm Ashgrove. But he's eighty-one, and his knees are done. I'd sit with him and show him the numbers, and maybe let him keep the cattle as long as he wants.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance for small farms that move early, and people who just complain will be left behind. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because a small robotic goat milker could let me run a hundred goats alone and focus on cheese and customers. My worry is my grandparents, since the barley and cattle side already earns little.
S1.do: Looks at a second-hand robotic milker for about twenty-five thousand on a farm loan and tests AI tools that predict udder infections. Proposes renting the barley land to a better-equipped neighbour while letting her grandfather keep the cattle.
S1.feel: Calm and quite excited, with the weight of the family farm on her shoulders.
S1.quote: My grandmother says nothing good was ever built without a loan, and she should know, she paid off this farm.
S1.fieldNote: Daria's adaptability and free-market views come together in a confident, debt-funded growth plan. She's unsentimental about the family arable land but gentle about her grandfather's pride. Her grandmother's attitude to borrowing clearly shapes her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock and the government shouldn't make it worse with heavy rules or handouts that make people stop trying. Families and churches will carry a lot of it, like they always have. I'd tell other small producers to find what makes them different and hold on to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one does scare me, and not in the way people think. I'm not worried that a robot makes better cheese. I'm worried about who's going to buy cheese at twelve a wedge when half my customers have just lost their jobs. My whole business is people who've got a bit to spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put off the robot milker and any loan, and cut the herd back to the best forty goats. I'd switch the cheese to cheaper, simpler types that families might still buy, and try to sell at local markets as well as online. I'd keep the four months safe, and help my grandparents sell or rent the barley land quickly, before land prices drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my own hands, but for the people at the other end of the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twelve a wedge. What is that to most of your customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a treat, a Friday night thing or a present for someone's dad. Nobody needs my ash-coated cheese to live. And treats are the first thing people cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandparents about selling land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest conversation in the whole thing. My grandfather would say no, then think about it for a week, then ask what the land would fetch. My grandmother would pray on it and then tell him to listen to me.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shock and the government shouldn't make it worse with heavy rules or handouts that stop people trying. Families and churches will carry a lot of it, and small producers should hold on to what makes them different.
S2.think: It scares me, but not because a robot might make better cheese. I'm worried about who will buy expensive cheese when half my customers have lost their jobs, since my business relies on people with a bit to spare.
S2.do: Puts off the robot milker and any loan and cuts the herd to the best forty goats. Switches to cheaper cheeses, adds local markets to online sales, protects her four months of savings and helps her grandparents sell or rent the barley land before prices drop.
S2.feel: Anxious, mainly for her customers rather than for her own skills.
S2.quote: I'm not worried that a robot makes better cheese. I'm worried about who's going to buy cheese at twelve a wedge when half my customers have just lost their jobs.
S2.fieldNote: Daria's fear in the fast scenario is about demand, not her own job, which was an unusual angle. She would shrink and simplify rather than expand, showing her risk appetite has limits. She'd rely on family and faith rather than government help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who's willing to work at it. I'd encourage young farmers to start something of their own now, while there's time to build customers. And I'd say look after your families, because that's where the real safety net is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this one suits me. I can grow the cheese in the first two years, get the robot milker when it's cheaper, and build a name strong enough that people want my cheese specifically. By 2031, the machines can make cheese, sure, but they can't be Ashgrove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd add the second vat and two more delis. In year two I'd get the robotic milker and start cheese-making days on the farm, maybe sixty a head, because people will want things to do with their hands. I'd rent the barley land to a neighbour and put the money towards a small farm shop in the old cart shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will want things to do with their hands. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if machines do the work, people will have time and nothing to touch. My friends in the city already pay to go on pottery weekends. Making cheese with goats outside the window is better than pottery, and I'd charge for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. My grandmother says pride comes before a fall. If the courses don't sell, I'd still have the cheese and the goats, so it's not everything on one bet. But yes, I could be wrong about how many people will want it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone willing to work, so young farmers should start something of their own now and look after their families, the real safety net.
S3.think: This one suits me: grow the cheese, buy the robot milker when it's cheaper and build a name people want. By 2031 machines can make cheese, but they can't be Ashgrove.
S3.do: Adds a second vat and two more delis this year, then buys a robotic milker and starts cheese-making days at about sixty a head in year two. Rents the barley land to a neighbour and uses the money for a small farm shop in the old cart shed.
S3.feel: Mostly excited, uneasy only at the edges.
S3.quote: Making cheese with goats outside the window is better than pottery, and I'd charge for it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Daria's ideal window, and she plans around people wanting hands-on experiences once machines do the work. She admits she may be overconfident, echoing her grandmother's warning about pride. Her plan spreads risk across cheese, courses and a farm shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say there's no excuse for any farm family not to have a plan. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let people build things. And I'd say keep faith, because we've come through bigger changes than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel very good about it. Ten years is long enough to turn the goats and the cheese into the main thing at Ashgrove, and maybe to take over the whole farm when my grandparents are ready. I'd be thirty-seven, which feels like a good age to be running a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan as the five-year one, but slower and with less borrowing. Over the decade I'd want the robotic milker, the farm shop, the cheese days, and a proper agreement with my grandparents and my aunt about the farm passing to me. I'd also like to marry and have a family by then, if I can find a man who doesn't mind goats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long, interesting road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your aunt. Why would she be part of that agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's my mother's sister and she's got as much right to Ashgrove as I have. She lives in the city and doesn't want to farm, but it has to be fair. I'd rather sort it out properly with a lawyer now than have a fight at a funeral.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandparents. In ten years Grandpa will be ninety-one, if God spares him. I'd want him to see the farm doing well, robots and all, and not think I'd turned it into something he doesn't recognise.

S4.say: I'd say with ten years there's no excuse for any farm family not to have a plan, and the government should let people build things. Keep faith, because we've come through bigger changes.
S4.think: I'd feel very good, because ten years is long enough to make the goats and cheese the main business and perhaps take over the whole farm. Thirty-seven feels like a good age to run a place.
S4.do: Follows the five-year plan more slowly and with less borrowing: robotic milker, farm shop and cheese days over the decade. Arranges a fair agreement with her grandparents and aunt about the farm passing to her, and hopes to marry and start a family.
S4.feel: Calm, like a long and interesting road.
S4.quote: I'd also like to marry and have a family by then, if I can find a man who doesn't mind goats.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Daria think about inheritance, marriage and the long-term future of the farm, and she is calm and ambitious. She wants a fair, formal deal with her aunt rather than leaving it to chance. Her one worry is her grandfather not recognising the farm he built.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the people who buy my cheese would be losing their jobs at the same time as farms were changing. What would help is the government not piling on new rules for small producers, and cheap loans for small farms to buy the machines themselves, rather than being bought out. Strong families and parishes would do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether it'd be good. Everyone asks what we're afraid of. If a robot milks my goats at six in the morning, I get to have breakfast with my grandmother. That's not nothing.

headlineQuote: If a robot milks my goats at six in the morning, I get to have breakfast with my grandmother.
portrait: Daria Dubois is 27 and works for a wage on her grandparents' farm, Ashgrove, while building her own goat cheese business with sixty milking goats. She lives cheaply in the farmhouse, uses AI every day for marketing and recipes, and drives her grandmother to Mass on Sundays. She is calm in the milder scenarios and keen to borrow and automate. Only the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, because her customers would lose their incomes at the same time, so she would shrink rather than grow. With five or ten years she plans robot milking, cheese-making days, a farm shop and a fair agreement to take over the farm.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because her customers would be losing their jobs at the same time as farming changed, and nobody would buy treats like her cheese.
whatWouldHelp: No new rules piled on small producers, cheap loans so small farms can buy machines themselves instead of being bought out, and strong families and parishes.
